performers: Odeon Grand Orchestra; conductor disputed (Friedrich Kark / Eduard Künneke)
intro: Odeon’s early recording of the first movement, Allegro con brio, of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67, was made through a recording horn onto shellac. It includes the four-note opening, the horn calls, the violin melody and the solo oboe passage.

sections.label: A · Three short notes and a hold
sections.mNote: The C-minor opening leads to a violin melody in E♭.

sections.label: B · Closing chords in E♭ major
sections.mNote: Repeated notes bring the exposition to its cadence.

sections.label: C · Winds and strings alternate single chords
D · Violin melody moving towards G
sections.mNote: F♯ moves to G before the C-major closing group.

cues.title: Opening motif, bars 1–5
cues.text: The famous opening begins with a quaver rest. Three Gs then fall to E♭, which is held under a fermata. Three Fs follow and fall to D.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, bars 1–5; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Second subject, first violins
cues.text: After the horn call, the first violins play the new theme in E♭ major, marked dolce. Below it the cellos repeat three short B♭s and a longer E♭, the rhythm of the opening motif.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 63–70; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Odeon recording on eight sides
cues.text: Odeon issued the complete symphony on eight sides, numbered 76147–76154. The labels named the company orchestra and did not name the conductor.
cues.evidence: James Hepokoski, ‘“Listen and Be Amazed!”: Odeon, Künneke, and the First Recordings of Complete Symphonies’, JAMS 76/1 (2023), pp. 113–167, identifies the eight sides, label credits and August 1911 sessions. He attributes the performance to Eduard Künneke; the archive transfer retains the older Kark/1910 identification. https://doi.org/10.1525/jams.2023.76.1.113

cues.title: Strings on D♭, bars 125–130
cues.text: The horns repeat B♭ and fall to G. The strings follow with three D♭s and a C, which clash briefly with the held horn note. The opening rhythm then begins to modulate.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 125–130; Mutopia 941, horns, strings and bassoons.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Alternating chords, winds and strings
cues.text: Winds and strings alternate single chords in minims, with a rest between each. Beethoven marks a diminuendo, then sempre più piano and pp.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 209–227; Mutopia 941, wind and string parts: minim replies, diminuendo, sempre più piano and pp.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Oboe Adagio, bar 268
cues.text: The orchestra stops after a G-major chord. The oboe continues alone, marked Adagio, descending through F, E♭ and D, then turning around the line before another held D.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bar 268; Mutopia 941, oboe solo marked Adagio and accompanying rests.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Horn call taken over by bassoons
cues.text: The bassoons take over the earlier horn call. Its new notes, G–G–G–C–D–G, prepare the violin melody in C major. The same tune is now a minor third lower.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 303–310; Mutopia 941, bassoon and first-violin parts; compare bars 59–66.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Pedal C in the violins
cues.text: The violins hold a high C while the bass moves beneath it through C, A♭, E and F. A cadence becomes the start of the coda. The final chords return the movement to C minor.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 374–381 and 491–502; Mutopia 941, strings.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
